dialogue.speaker: sea-cartographer
dialogue.text: A market carrier says the roof-shaped mark takes her straight to Lantern House. A deckhand wants the two lights she was shown from the skiff. Clip one mark onto this plain shore sketch. Both readers will use the same sheet from the same bench. Then try the other mark.

options.text: Pin the stepped roof mark to the sketch.
Pin two light dots in the same place.
Leave both marks on the desk.

dialogue.speaker: sea-cartographer
dialogue.text: The carrier points to the step in the roof and names Lantern House. The deckhand points farther up the page. “That could be the store roof from where I work.” The sheet, bench and readers will stay the same for the next mark.

options.text: Leave the copy on the desk.
Clear the mark and keep the same sheet.

dialogue.speaker: sea-cartographer
dialogue.text: With the two dots on the same sheet, the deckhand names the pair of lights on the upper landing. The carrier asks whether the dots show two buildings. Renna tells you the shore frame can check where both first choices were meant to point.

options.text: Leave the copy on the desk.
Clear the mark and keep the same sheet.

dialogue.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
dialogue.text: You found both marks on the same landing from the shore frame. The roof and the lights each helped one reader. Put a key where someone can learn the other mark without guessing. Keep Lantern House in words alongside both.

options.text: Put both marks by Market Rail.
Put both marks by the skiff.

dialogue.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
dialogue.text: A carrier shows a new reader the roof cutout on the rail. They use the words beside it to match the two dots on the copy a deckhand carried up the steps. The key meets them before the turn to the market.

dialogue.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
dialogue.text: A deckhand uses the key to show a passenger which upper landing will show both lights. The passenger matches the roof mark from her shore copy. The key will be there when the crew begins the next handover.

dialogue.speaker: sea-cartographer
dialogue.text: The museum records how dugouts helped Yanyuwa crews reach nearby islands. Rra-Kalwanyimara keeps a place reference in its name. Our skiff’s crew painted Glint inside its hull. Move Glint’s name to the boat line on this practice sheet and give the loading step its own position.

options.text: Use the Cold Store tabs to separate the boat name and the loading step.
Use two chart-room slips for the boat name and the loading step.
Leave the old key on the desk.

dialogue.speaker: sea-cartographer
dialogue.text: The boat token can move when the crew reties it. Salt Step stays under the rail. One line keeps a name with the vessel. The other tells a porter where to go for the next load.

dialogue.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
dialogue.text: People waiting uphill can use a wide key at the rail. The next carrier arrives with a crate and needs the loading mark beside the skiff. Either copy can lead back to the chart-room name line. Where do you want the next person to see the key?

options.text: Pin the full name and loading directions to Market Rail.
Clip a point-of-use strip at the skiff and keep the name file in Lantern House.
Leave both clips for the next round.

dialogue.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
dialogue.text: A porter reads Salt Step uphill and follows the rail there. The boat name stays above the moveable token. A new mooring needs a new loading line.

dialogue.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
dialogue.text: A carrier can read Salt Step from the path beside the skiff. A small arrow sends anyone asking where Glint got its name to Renna’s chart-room file.

missions.title: A Roof and Two Lights
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What helps people connect an unfamiliar mark to the place it stands for?

objectives.title: Try both marks with the two readers and check their landmark at the shore frame.
Leave both marks and the landmark’s name where people can use the key.

missions.title: A Name That Travels
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What can a name tell us about a place and where does someone need a direction?

objectives.title: Read the named canoe’s record, then check Glint’s crew and Salt Step.
Move the boat token and give the loading step its own map line.
Place the new key and trace it to the next loading step.

hints.text: Readers can know different marks for one landmark.
Look for Renna’s symbol desk in Lantern House.
Put the roof mark and the two dots on the same sketch. Listen to both readers.
After both trials, go to Seagrass Steps and look through the shore sight frame by the market.
Give the reader the place name alongside the mark they recognise.
Find the empty key holder at Seagrass Steps.
Choose who will reach the key first, the carriers at Market Rail or the readers boarding the skiff.
Hang the key at the rail or at the skiff. Read the new sign at your chosen place.
Someone read a boat’s name as the name of a loading step.
The named canoe’s museum record is in Lantern House.
Find the crew’s token at Shoal Shelf and the loading slip at Seagrass Steps.
Find what each record points to. A vessel can move while loading steps stay in place.
The same line on an old map can make two things look like one.
Return to Renna’s two rails in Lantern House.
Give Glint’s token and Salt Step separate positions with the Cold Store tabs or Renna’s spare slips.
Bring the separate lines to Sora at the Seagrass rail.
Someone needs a direction while carrying a crate.
Visit Sora’s rail at Seagrass Steps.
Put the complete key at Market Rail or a short strip near the skiff.
Read the chosen key and follow it to Salt Step to see where the next load went.

sources.title: Australian National Maritime Museum, Dugout Canoe Rra-Kalwanyimara, 00001826
sources.locator: Dugout Canoe description and fields for date, medium, manufacturers, language and clan
sources.supports: The museum records this silver paperbark dugout as made in 1988 by Annie Karrakayn, Ida Ninganga and Issac Walayunkuma. It gives Yanyuwa for the first two and Garrawa for the third. Its public description attributes an account of linking boat names to country to Annie Karrakayn and relates this name to Kalwanyi. It describes how dugouts extended Yanyuwa access to nearby islands.

cards.title: Rra-Kalwanyimara, Sea Museum object 00001826
cards.text: The Australian National Maritime Museum records this silver paperbark dugout as made by Annie Karrakayn and Ida Ninganga, who were Yanyuwa, and Issac Walayunkuma, who was Garrawa. In its published account Annie explains why a boat’s name can keep a place with it. This canoe’s name refers to Kalwanyi.
cards.limits: The record names a particular boat and its makers. It gives no route through the fictional harbour. Its teaching picture is a generic hull outline.

exhibits.name: The Rra-Kalwanyimara museum record
exhibits.dateKind: The date given for the commissioned museum canoe.
exhibits.summary: Australian National Maritime Museum object 00001826 is a dugout made of silver paperbark. It was commissioned in 1987 and is dated 1988. The museum links the recorded name to Kalwanyi.
